/Through Tuesday/...
Issued at 1123 PM MST Tue Nov 3 2026

We are expecting a quiet overnight with mostly clear skies. Skies 
will be partly cloudy in the morning with increasing clouds by 
Wednesday afternoon for the high country, Denver metro, and the 
adjacent plains. Temperatures will top out in the mid to upper 50s 
for the plains once again. The trough and associated low are 
currently over Nevada. As this feature moves east, it will bring us 
the 2nd storm system of the week, which will quickly move through 
our area on Wednesday afternoon and into Wednesday night. We expect 
the highest impacts for the central and southern high country. 

Precipitation will increase from west to east starting mid afternoon 
on Wednesday in the high country. The precipitation shield should 
shift south and east through Wednesday evening and into the 
overnight. On Wednesday evening, scattered rain showers and perhaps 
a few snowflakes mixing in are possible for the Palmer Divide. There 
is a low but nonzero chance (~10-15%) that this potential could even 
extend into far southern and western parts of the Denver metro. No 
snow accumulation is expected in these locations. Some rain showers 
are possible for southern Lincoln County late Wednesday night into 
early Thursday morning as the low pushes off to the east of our area.

High resolution model guidance has shown an uptick in moisture 
compared to model runs over the last 24-36 hours. As the afternoon 
progresses on Wednesday, there should be some modest instability 
present in the southern high country along with increasing lapse 
rates. Snow levels are trending lower as well. Snow levels should 
start around 9,000 feet early Wednesday afternoon. They are now 
forecast to drop down to 7,500-8,000 feet on Wednesday evening. Snow 
levels should drop even lower to 6,500-7,000 feet just as the system 
starts to exit the area early Thursday AM. The track of the low 
across our southwestern counties or just to the south would bring 
northeast to east winds at the surface. This flow could extend up in 
the atmosphere a few kilometers. In this type of flow, Park County 
looks favored for some upslope flow/enhancement. In particular, the 
southern Front Range foothills, the Mosquito Range, the Highway 285 
corridor, and most of Park County look favored for the heaviest 
snowfall totals from this system.

Altogether, most short-term models have trended up with snowfall 
totals and QPF in the last 24-36 hours. QPF amounts of 0.25-0.75" 
should be common in Park County and adjacent locations with isolated 
higher amounts possible at the highest elevations. DESI 
probabilities are honing in on the Mosquito Range/western Park 
County where there is a 50-60% chance that these locations receive 6 
inches or more of snowfall. Thus, we have issued a Winter Weather 
Advisory for the mountains of Summit County, Park County, the 
Mosquito Range, Indian Peaks, and South Park. It runs from 2pm 
Wednesday to 2am Thursday. Most of Park County should get 3+ inches 
snowfall with the Mosquito Range forecast to receive 5-10 inches of 
snowfall with localized higher amounts possible. Areas along and 
adjacent to the I-70 corridor above 7,500 feet, including the 
northern Gore Range, are forecast to get 3-6 inches of snowfall with 
areas to the north getting much less.

There is still good agreement that ridging aloft moves back in for 
Thursday followed by a trough passing to our north on Friday. This 
system will lack moisture for our area. As a result, there are only 
low precipitation chances for Friday afternoon in the high country. 
Temperatures are forecast to reach the mid to upper 50s for the 
plains on Thursday and Friday. Ridging resumes once again for the 
weekend and into next week. We expect dry conditions across our area 
from Saturday through the end of the forecast period. The ridge is 
expected to strengthen and the center should move closer to us for 
the end of the weekend and into early next week. Mid 60s look 
increasingly likely for Denver for Sunday and Monday according to 
ensemble guidance. This would be 5-10 degrees above average for this 
time of year. Temperatures on the eastern plains could even be 
pushing 70 F. For Tuesday, more zonal flow could be in place 
dropping high temperatures back into the low 60s for most of the 
plains.
